title: Zoom in: the API's admission decision, cheapest rejection first
caption: Three questions, all answered locally in microseconds: token, estimated wait, and room in the queue.

steps.text: An order arrives at the Checkout API.
It carries a valid, unexpired token from the waiting room.
Estimate its wait: queue depth ÷ drain rate (Little's law). 600 orders at 100/s is 6 s, well under the client's 30 s timeout.
The queue is below its bound.
Enqueue it and answer 202 with an order id the client can poll.

scenarios.name: Queue full
scenarios.summary: At the bound, a new order is rejected in a millisecond with a hint for when to retry, instead of waiting to fail.

steps.text: Same checks: valid token, estimated wait under the deadline.
The queue holds 2 000 orders: it is full.
A new order doesn't hold seats yet, so it gets no reserved space.
503 with Retry-After: 15, plus jitter on the client so retries don't arrive together.

scenarios.name: Drain slows
scenarios.summary: When workers slow down, the estimated wait crosses the deadline before the queue is even full, and admission stops early.

steps.text: Payment is slow, so the drain rate falls from 100/s to 20/s.
1 000 queued orders at 20/s is a 50 s wait, longer than the 30 s client timeout.
Reject now: the order would expire in the queue and its work would be wasted.

scenarios.name: Held seats, queue full
scenarios.summary: Shed the cheapest work first: a buyer already holding seats is finishing a sale, so it may use a small reserved slice.

steps.text: The queue is full, but this request confirms payment for seats the buyer already holds.
10% of capacity is reserved for this kind of request, so it is admitted.
Without the reservation the hold would expire and the seats would go back on sale unpaid.
